tasks.title: Oral exam: show it, describe it, defend it
tasks.prompt: As if presenting to an examiner: (1) show the most important lung nodule with an arrow, (2) describe it in one sentence (location, size, pattern), (3) give your leading interpretation with the image evidence for it, and (4) explain why a pulmonary vessel seen end-on or a granuloma is less likely. Then name the other major abnormality on this study.

hints.text: Keep it to four sentences. Examiners reward a clear search pattern and an honest statement of what the images cannot tell you (growth over time cannot be judged from one study).

tasks.explanation: There is no automatic grader for free-text reasoning. Compare your answer with the checklist and the linked book pages.

rubric.text: Showed the finding on the right series and slice
One-sentence description with location, size and pattern
Leading interpretation supported by named image features
Closest alternative (a pulmonary vessel seen end-on or a granuloma) addressed with opposing evidence
Stated what needs comparison, other sequences/phases, or clinical information
Also reported the large right pleural effusion with compressive collapse (atelectasis) of the adjacent right lung.

tasks.title: Judge the technical quality
tasks.prompt: Before reading the lungs, assess this frontal radiograph's technique: projection, inspiration (count posterior ribs), rotation (spinous processes vs clavicle heads) and penetration.

hints.text: A good inspiration shows about 9–10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm; rotation shifts the spinous processes away from the midpoint between the clavicle heads.

tasks.explanation: Technique changes appearances: poor inspiration crowds the bases and widens the heart; rotation distorts the mediastinum; AP projection magnifies the heart.

rubric.text: Projection stated (PA or as recorded)
Inspiration judged by counting posterior ribs
Rotation judged with spinous processes and clavicle heads
Penetration judged (spine visible through the heart?)

tasks.title: Trace the cardiomediastinal borders
tasks.prompt: Place named arrows on each segment of the right and left cardiomediastinal borders (e.g. SVC, right atrium, aortic knob, main pulmonary artery, left ventricle) and say whether any segment looks abnormal.

hints.text: Right border, top to bottom: SVC, then right atrium. Left border: aortic knob, main pulmonary artery, then left ventricle.

tasks.explanation: No anatomical reference outlines exist for this radiograph, so compare your arrows with the book's figure of the normal contours and self-review.

rubric.text: Right border: SVC identified, and noted that the right heart border (right atrium) is hidden by the right-sided pleural opacity (silhouette sign)
Left border: aortic knob, main pulmonary artery and left ventricle identified
Commented on whether any segment bulges or is effaced

tasks.title: Measure the cardiothoracic ratio
tasks.prompt: Use the Length tool (L) to measure the widest heart diameter and the widest inner thoracic diameter, then state the ratio and whether this projection allows a judgement of heart size.

hints.text: Measure the heart from its rightmost to leftmost point; the thorax at its widest inner rib margins, usually at the domes of the diaphragm.

tasks.explanation: The ratio is a heuristic for PA films; on AP films the heart is magnified, so an apparently large ratio is not reliable. Detector-plane pixel spacing is not patient-calibrated, but a ratio cancels that scale.

rubric.text: Recognised that the right heart border is hidden by the right-sided pleural opacity, so the heart width cannot be measured reliably on this film
Ratio given only with that caveat, or stated as not measurable
Projection caveat stated (PA: usable)
